name: Uluburun
political_setting: Off the Anatolian coast; cargo and personal effects connect Cypriot, Levantine, Egyptian, and Aegean worlds.
anchor_label: approximately 10 tonnes copper plus 1 tonne tin
carrier: elite or official shipment; ownership unresolved
evidence: A single wreck preserves bulk copper and tin, at least 149 Canaanite jars, luxury materials, balance weights, personal gear, and a Lebanese-cedar hull.
interpretation: Bulk materials, containers, elite goods, crew possessions, and passengers converged in one voyage; that mixture does not identify one owner or one commercial institution.
limits: Uluburun is one exceptional late-fourteenth-century wreck, not a representative cargo, annual flow, standard route, or proof that a palace owned every item aboard. The vessel's departure, stops, destination, ownership, and institutional status remain debated.

name: Cape Gelidonya
political_setting: Off Lycia; a Cypro-Levantine interpretation is plausible, but the wreck cannot be assigned securely to one polity or crew identity.
anchor_label: documented copper-ingot fragments; at least one-third of the shipment
carrier: probable travelling metalworker or freelance merchant
evidence: Copper and tin ingots, Cypriot scrap bronze, weights, hammerstones, polishers, a whetstone, and a possible stone anvil survive together.
interpretation: The working tools and fragmented metal make a travelling tinker or freelance metal venture the best current interpretation, materially different from Uluburun's elite cargo.
limits: The tinker model is an interpretation, not a named occupation from a text. More than 750 fragments are not 750 complete ingots or a full shipment count, and the ship's Canaanite, Cypriot, or other identity is unresolved.

name: Point Iria
political_setting: Inside the Mycenaean Argolid, yet the surviving containers combine Cypriot, Cretan, and mainland Mycenaean pottery traditions.
anchor_label: Cypriot, Cretan, and mainland Mycenaean ceramic traditions
carrier: mixed coasting cargo; vessel identity unresolved
evidence: The recovered cargo is dominated by storage and transport pottery: Cypriot pithoi, Cretan transport stirrup jars, mainland Mycenaean vessels, and smaller cooking or serving wares.
interpretation: A relatively modest, mixed container cargo shows regional exchange continuing near 1200 BCE without requiring a royal convoy or one culturally homogeneous ship.
limits: Ceramic origins do not identify crew ethnicity, ownership, a complete itinerary, or the vanished organic contents. Proposed Cyprus-to-Crete-to-Argolid movement is a reconstruction rather than an observed sequence of stops.

name: Kommos
political_setting: A harbor on southern Crete within changing Minoan and Mycenaean political settings; imported material reached the site across those transitions.
anchor_label: ceramic fragments in one neutron-activation sample
evidence: A targeted neutron-activation study tested 69 fragments thought to be Cypriot or Mycenaean imports; roughly 80 percent supported those regional identifications. Excavations also recovered Levantine and Egyptian transport vessels.
interpretation: Kommos worked as an interface where imported containers, local households, storage, and visiting ships met; an archaeological sample makes contact visible without counting traffic.
limits: The 69 fragments are a deliberately selected analytical sample, not all pottery at Kommos, a share of imports, a count of ships, or an annual series. Roughly 80 percent validates classifications within that sample only.

name: Hala Sultan Tekke
political_setting: A Cypriot harbor city whose imported pottery and luxury goods connect Aegean, Anatolian, Levantine, Egyptian, and Sardinian contexts.
carrier: port city, producers, merchants, and households
evidence: Scientific analyses and excavations identify imports from across the eastern Mediterranean and as far as Sardinia, alongside urban copper and purple-dye production at a city of at least 25 hectares.
interpretation: The port linked local production to multiple supplier and consumer regions over centuries; it was an inhabited industrial city rather than a single palace warehouse or cargo event.
limits: The minimum city extent and list of provenances do not measure simultaneous population, annual imports, export volume, market share, or direct sailings. Finds span multiple contexts and centuries and cannot be collapsed into one typical year.
